To use bisogna / è necessario / occorre + infinitive for a general rule.
To use bisogna che / è necessario che + subjunctive for a particular person.
To use "dovere" in the present, the conditional (dovrei) and the past.
To express need with servire, occorrere, avere bisogno di.
To give advice with conviene, è meglio che, sarebbe meglio.
To explain formal rules: è obbligatorio, è vietato, essere tenuto a.
Florence, 1st September, nine o'clock. Matei and Giulia's first day as directors of the workshop, and Chiara's first day as a restorer.
Good morning, directors! What do I have to do first?
Please, no "directors". Let's use "tu", we're colleagues.
First of all you have to sign the contract. Then you need to read the safety regulations.
All of it? It's forty pages!
I'm afraid so. It has to be read by law. And with solvents it's compulsory to wear a mask.
And on Saturdays we have to open at nine on the dot. Pietro is extremely strict.
And the coffee? I've heard that at ten it's compulsory.
That's the most important rule of all. Graziella doesn't forgive.
We also have to send the monthly report to the Heritage Authority by Friday. Who's writing it?
There's no need to look at me. I wrote it last time.
Then it's better if Chiara writes it. She writes formal letters better than all of us.
There's no need to tell me twice. But first it's better if I see the paintings.
Right. First you look. Then you write.
"bisogna che" = it's necessary that, have to
"non serve che" = there's no need to
"non c’è bisogno che" = there's no need to
For a general rule that applies to everyone, use these impersonal expressions + INFINITIVE:
You need to wear a mask.
We have to open at nine.
"Bisogna" never has a subject and isn't conjugated: it's always "bisogna" (past "bisognava", future "bisognerà").
When the obligation concerns a particular person, add "che" + SUBJUNCTIVE:
Chiara needs to read the regulations.
Someone had to open the door.
With some verbs the indicative and subjunctive forms are the same ("tu firmi"). Watch the verbs where they differ: "bisogna che tu VADA", NOT "vai"; "è necessario che io SIA", NOT "sono".
I have to write the report.
I was supposed to leave, but I stayed.
I had to call the locksmith.
"Dovevo" = that was the plan, but maybe it didn't happen. "Ho dovuto" = it really happened, I had no choice.
4. Need: servire, occorrere, avere bisogno di
"Servire" and "occorrere" agree with the thing you need (which is the subject):
Non c’è bisogno che tu venga.
There's no need for you to come.
NOT "Mi serve due pennelli". The verb agrees: "Mi SERVONO due pennelli" (like "mi piacciono").
Il personale è tenuto a indossare la mascherina.
On Italian signs you'll often see: "È vietato l’ingresso", "È obbligatorio l’uso del casco", "Si prega di non toccare".
Three signatures are needed for this form.
Yesterday I had to call the locksmith.
Non c’è bisogno che tu vieni.

First you look. Then you write.

On the first of September, at half past eight in the morning, Matei and Giulia were standing in front of the workshop door, with Viola in her pram and Ernesto's old iron key in hand. It was a solemn moment. Giulia had even put on her green dress, the one from her first day at the Uffizi. Matei put the key in the lock, took a deep breath and turned. The key didn't move.

He tried again. Nothing. He tried left, right, pushing, pulling. Nothing. "You need to turn it more gently," Giulia suggested. "What I need is for you not to tell me how to turn a key," Matei replied, beginning to sweat. Viola, in her pram, was watching the scene with great interest, as if it were a show put on for her.

At ten to nine Chiara arrived, as punctual as a Swiss watch. At five to nine Pietro arrived, who wasn't even supposed to be there, because school started the next day. And at nine on the dot, by chance, an elegant gentleman with his hands behind his back walked past, who lived two streets away and was apparently taking a stroll.

"Good morning," said Bellini, innocently. "Problems?" "The key won't turn," Matei admitted. Bellini took the key, put it in the lock, pulled it back a millimetre, turned it with a short sharp jerk, and the door opened. "You have to pull it back a little," he explained. "My grandfather did it that way for sixty years. Didn't I tell you? How careless of me." Then he walked off, whistling, without looking back.

The first week was the hardest of their professional lives. Nobody had warned them that running a workshop mainly meant filling in forms. You needed one form to receive a painting, another to return it, a third to buy solvents and a fourth to dispose of them. Every form needed three signatures, two stamps and, according to Matei, a miracle.

On Tuesday a painting arrived from a church in Prato, a small sixteenth-century Annunciation, with a letter from the parish priest saying: "It must be ready by the eighth of December, the feast of the Immaculate Conception." On Wednesday the Heritage Authority phoned to remind them that the monthly report had to be handed in by Friday, "no exceptions". On Thursday the solvent supplier announced that, by law, someone had to attend a sixteen-hour safety course.

The Annunciation was entrusted to Chiara. It was her first real job, and she looked at it for a whole morning before touching it. Then she wrote down in a notebook everything that needed doing: cleaning the yellowed varnish, consolidating two cracks in the wood, retouching a small loss in the angel's wing. At the bottom of the page she added: "Needed: patience, three months and a very small brush." Giulia read the list and knew they had chosen well.

"But how did Bellini manage?" Giulia asked on Thursday evening at the kitchen table, among mountains of paper. "Forty years of this. And he still had time to restore." Matei shrugged. "Maybe he didn't fill anything in. Maybe he put it all in a drawer and waited for it to go away." Graziella, bringing the coffee, laughed. "Drawer, my foot. Bellini filled everything in at night. I used to see him from my window: the light in his study stayed on until two."

Giulia attended the sixteen-hour safety course, on Saturday and Sunday, in a cold classroom on the outskirts of the city, with plumbers, decorators and a locksmith who slept in the front row. You had to learn by heart the symbols for dangerous products, the rules for fire extinguishers and the safety distances. At the end there was an exam. Giulia passed with the highest mark. The locksmith, woken at the last minute, came second.

Meanwhile, every morning at nine on the dot, Bellini walked past the workshop "by chance". On Tuesday he stopped to look at the Prato painting through the window. On Wednesday he suggested, without anyone asking him, that it would be better to use a lighter solvent for the varnish on the cloak. On Thursday he brought croissants. On Friday he came in, sat down in his old corner and said: "There's no need to worry. I'm not here. Pretend I'm not here."

Viola had her place in the workshop too. Giulia brought her in the mornings and put her in a little playpen by the window, with a sheet of paper and some wax crayons. She wasn't allowed to touch the paintings, of course, and Viola seemed to know it. She drew for hours, in silence, big patches of colour that she called, depending on the day, "Totò", "nonno" or "guadda". Chiara said they were the most abstract drawings she had ever seen.

Chiara wrote the monthly report, as planned. It was perfect: three clear, orderly pages, with all the right formulas and not a single mistake. Matei read it twice, then passed it to Giulia. "We need to give her a raise," he said. "First she needs to finish her probation," Giulia replied, laughing. "But yes, you're right."

On Friday afternoon Davide arrived with a long, flat parcel wrapped in brown paper. He had been working on it all week, secretly, in the cellar at home. Inside was a wooden nameplate, hand-painted, with gold lettering. It read: "Ernesto Bellini Restoration Workshop". And underneath, smaller: "Directors: M. Popa and G. Esposito". And further down, very small, almost hidden in the corner: "Look. And don't touch anything."

Bellini, from his corner, saw the nameplate and slowly stood up. "My grandfather's name on the door," he said. "That wasn't necessary." "Yes, it was," Giulia replied. "It's the most necessary thing of all." Bellini didn't say anything. He just took out his handkerchief and blew his nose, for a long time, looking out of the window.

That evening, after hanging the nameplate with the help of Pietro, who held the ladder, Matei and Giulia talked for a long time. "We need to find him something to do," said Giulia. "He can't walk past the door every morning pretending to be there by chance." "We could ask him to teach Davide on Saturdays," said Matei. "Officially. With a title." "What title?" Matei thought about it. "Consultant. The Saturday consultant."

On Monday morning, at ten to nine, Bellini found a formal letter under the door, written by Chiara with all the right formulas: "Dear Professor, we are pleased to inform you of your appointment as consultant to the workshop. You are required to present yourself every Saturday at nine o'clock. Arriving late is forbidden. Drinking coffee at ten is compulsory. Yours sincerely." Bellini read it on the pavement, once, twice. Then he knocked on the door, like a guest. Matei opened it. "Good morning, consultant," he said. And this time the key turned first time.
